implementation_notes: Java is where lava flow is most visible, because Java generations live side by side: Jackson and Gson, or Jackson's annotations alongside a different databind configuration, Spring MVC and WebFlux, JPA and hand-written JDBC, Log4j 1.x and SLF4J wrappers over both. The dependencies and the incoming fan grow with each migration layer, and the knowledge is fragmented. The remediation is Java-specific and mechanical: an enforcer rule in the build that fails on the legacy import, so the migration has a completion mechanism, plus a deprecation cycle to drive the count down.
idiom_name: Jackson and Gson; Spring MVC and WebFlux; JPA and JDBC
code_sketch:
<!-- the migration needs a completion mechanism, not a plan -->
<plugin>enforcer</plugin>
<rules>
  <bannedDependencies><excludes><exclude>com.google.code.gson:gson</exclude></excludes>
</plugin>
pitfalls: Jackson's polymorphic typing being enabled in one module and not another is a security concern layered on top of the coexistence.
Mixing JPA and JDBC in the same transaction means two connection pools and two transaction managers, which is a much harder problem than the migration.
Both Spring MVC and WebFlux on the classpath causes both stacks to initialise, and the failure appears as a slow, confusing startup.
